The political event-study results are sensitive to baseline controls. More trade-exposed CZs show a more positive Republican presidential-margin association in minimally controlled specifications for 2016 and 2020, relative to 1988, but this pattern largely disappears with core controls and turns slightly negative and statistically indistinguishable from zero with full controls. We therefore do not find a robust positive relationship across specifications, let alone establish a causal effect of import exposure on Republican voting.

This sensitivity highlights the role of pre-existing local industry and demographic characteristics in interpreting political trajectories. Our CZ-level exposure design differs from the instrumental-variables analysis of labor-market outcomes in ADH, and the strength of an exposure first stage does not resolve the political design's identification assumptions. Moreover, commuting-zone outcomes cannot reveal how individual voters changed their preferences or whether changes arose through turnout, migration, or party composition.

Trade shocks remain a relevant setting for studying local political change, but the present evidence is conditional on specification and cannot isolate a mechanism. Future research combining individual-level political behavior with migration, registration, turnout, and political-supply measures could help distinguish those channels.
